transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Good morning, Kenton Festival box office. How can I help you?

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Oh, good morning. I'm coming to Kenton for a few days' holiday next month, and a friend told me there's a festival. She gave me this number to find out about it.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: That's right, the festival begins on the 16th of May and goes on till the 19th.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Oh, that's great. I'll be there from the 15th till the 19th. So could you tell me the programme, please?

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Well, on the first day, there's the opening ceremony, in the town centre. People start gathering around 2 o'clock, to get a good place to see from, and <q id="1">the events will start at 2.45,</q> and finish about 5.30.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: OK, thanks. I'll make sure I get there early to get a good spot.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: The festival will be officially opened by the mayor. He'll just speak for a few minutes, welcoming everyone to the festival. All the town councillors will be there, and of course lots of other people.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: <q id="2">Then there'll be a performance by a band.</q> Most years we have a children's choir, but this year the local army cadets offered to perform, and they're very good.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Uhhuh.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: <q id="3">After that, a community group from the town will perform a play they've written themselves, just a short one. It's about Helen Tungate.</q> I don't know if you've heard of her?

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: I certainly have. <q id="4">She was a scientist years ago.</q>

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: That's right. She was born in Kenton exactly 100 years ago, so we're celebrating her centenary.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: I'm a biologist, so I've always been interested in her. I didn't realise she came from Kenton.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Yes. Well, all that will take place in the afternoon, and <q id="5">later, as the sun sets, there'll be a firework display. You should go to the park to watch, as you'll get the best view from there, and the display takes place on the opposite side of the river.</q> It's always one of the most popular events in the festival.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Sounds great.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: And what's happening on the other days?

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: There are several events that go on the whole time. For example, <q id="6">the students of the art college have produced a number of videos, all connected with relationships between children and their grandparents.</q>

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: That sounds interesting. It makes a change from children and parents, doesn't it!

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Exactly. Because the art college is in use for classes, throughout the festival, <q id="7">the videos are being shown in Handsworth House.</q>

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: How do you spell the name?

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: H-A-N-D-S-W-O-R-T-H. Handsworth House. It's close to the Town Hall.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Now let me see, what else can I tell you about?

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Are there any displays of ballet dancing? I'm particularly interested in that as I do it as a hobby.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: There isn't any ballet, I'm afraid, but <q id="8">there'll be a demonstration of traditional dances from all round the country.</q>

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Oh, that'd be nice. Where's that being held?

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: <q id="9">It's in the market in the town centre – the outdoor one, not the covered market.</q> And it's on at 2 and 5 every afternoon of the festival, apart from the first day.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Lovely. I'm interested in all kinds of dancing, so I'm sure I'll enjoy that!

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Mmm. I'm sure you will.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: And I'd really like to go to some concerts, if there are any.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Yes, there are several. Three performed by professionals, and one by local children.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: And where is it being held?

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: It's in the library, which is in Park Street. On the 18th, at 6.30 in the evening.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: I presume I'll need tickets for that.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: <q id="10">Yes, you can book online, or you can buy them when you arrive in Kenton, either at the festival box office, or from any shops displaying our logo in the windows.</q>

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Well, I think that'll keep me busy for the whole of my stay in Kenton. Thank you so much for all your help.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: You're welcome. I hope you enjoy your stay.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Thank you. Goodbye.
Right. I've now almost succeeded in finalising plans for our tour, so I'll bring you up to date with what I know.
As you know, we're flying first to Munich, on Monday the 4th.

The flight is at 11.30, so it's too early to have lunch at the airport. <q id="11">I suggest we meet there for coffee at 10, which should give us plenty of time for breakfast before we leave home.</q>

<q id="12">When we arrive in Munich, we'll be met at the airport by Claus Bauer. Claus works for a tour operator, and he'll look after us for the time we'll be in Germany. He's already liaised with the managers of the theatres we're going to visit, and he's also arranged for an officer of the National Theatre in Munich to show us round the theatre one afternoon during our stay.</q>

Now last time we discussed this trip, I didn't have the precise cost for hotel rooms, but now I have. <q id="13">The normal rate at the hotel where we're staying is 150 euros a night for a double room. I'd hoped to get that down to 120 euros, but in fact I've been able to negotiate a rate of 110.</q> That'll be reflected in the final payment which you'll need to make by the end of this week.

On Tuesday, the day after our arrival, I had hoped we could sit in on a rehearsal at one of the theatres, but unfortunately that's proved very difficult to arrange, so instead we'll have a coach trip to one of the amazing castles in the mountains south of Munich.

On Tuesday evening, we'll all have dinner together in a restaurant near our hotel. From talking to you all about your preferences, it was clear that a typical local restaurant would be too meat-oriented for some of you. <q id="14">Some of you suggested an Italian restaurant, but I must confess that I decided to book a Lebanese one, as we have plenty of opportunities to go to an Italian restaurant at home.</q>

<q id="15">On Wednesday afternoon, the director of the play we're going to see that evening will talk to us at the theatre.</q> She'll describe the whole process of producing a play, including how she chose the actors, and, as the play we're going to see is a modern one, how she worked with the playwright.
Right. Now I'd just like to make a few points about the plays we're going to see, partly because it might influence your choice of clothes to take with you!

<q id="16">The play we're seeing on Wednesday evening is a modern one, and we're going to the premiere,</q> so it'll be quite a dressy occasion, though of course you don't have to dress formally. I gather it's rather a multimedia production, with amazing lighting effects and a soundtrack of electronic music, though unfortunately the playwright is ill and is unlikely to be able to attend.

<q id="17">On Thursday we're seeing a play that was first performed last year, when it was commissioned to mark a hundred years since the birth in the town of a well-known scientist.</q> We're going to see a revival of that production, which aroused a lot of interest.

<q id="18">Friday's play will really make you think hard about what clothes to pack, as it'll be in the garden of a palace.</q> It's a beautiful setting, but I'd better warn you, there won't be much protection from the wind.

<q id="19">On Saturday, we're going by coach to a theatre in another town, not far from Munich. This will be the opening of a drama festival, and the mayor and all the other dignitaries of the town will be attending.</q> After the performance, the mayor is hosting a reception for all the audience, and there'll be a band playing traditional music of the region.

And after having a day off on Sunday, <q id="20">our final play is on Monday, and it's in the stunning setting of the old Town Hall, which dates back to the 14th century.</q> The performance marks the fifty years that the lead actor has been on stage, and the play is the one where he made his first professional appearance, all those years ago.
And the day after that, we'll be flying back home. Now have you got any questions before I ...

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: Oh good morning. You must be James. I'm Beth Cartwright – please call me Beth.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: Now as this is your first tutorial since you started on the Scandinavian Studies course, I'd like to find out something about you. Why did you decide to take this course?

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: <q id="21">Well, my mother is Danish, and although we always lived in England, she used to talk about her home a lot, and that made me want to visit Denmark. We hardly ever did, though – my mother usually went on her own. But whenever her relations or friends were in England they always came to see us.</q>

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: I see. So I assume you already speak Danish, one of the languages you'll be studying.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: I can get by when I talk to people, though I'm not terribly accurate.

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: Now you probably know that you'll spend the third year of the course abroad. Have you had any thoughts about that?

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: I'm really looking forward to it. And although Denmark seems the obvious place to go, because of my family connections, I'd love to spend the time in Iceland.

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: Oh, I'm sure it can be arranged. Do you have any plans for when you graduate? A lot of students go on to take a master's degree.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: I think the four years of the undergraduate course will be enough for me. <q id="22">I'm interested in journalism, and I quite like the idea of moving to Scandinavia and writing for magazines.</q> I'd find that more creative than translating, which I suppose most graduates do.

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: OK. Now how are you finding the courses you're taking this term, James?

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: Well, I'm really enjoying the one on Swedish cinema.

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: <q id="23">That'll continue next term, but the one on Scandinavian literature that's running at the moment will be replaced by more specialised courses.</q> Oh, and by the way, if you're interested in watching Danish television programmes – there's going to be a course on that the term after next.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: That sounds good.

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: Have you started thinking about the literature paper that you have to write in the next few weeks?

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: Yes, my first choice would be to do something on the Icelandic sagas.

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: Hmm. The trouble with that is that a lot of people choose that topic, and it can be difficult to get hold of the books you'll need. Why not leave that for another time?

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: <q id="24">You might find modern novels or 19th century playwrights interesting.</q>

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: <q id="24">I've read or seen several plays in translation, so that would be a good idea.</q>

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: Fine. I'll put you down for that topic.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: Right. So what would you advise me to aim at in the paper?

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: First I suggest you avoid taking one writer and going into a great deal of detail. That approach certainly has its place, but <q id="25">I think you first need to get an understanding of the literature in the context of the society in which it was produced – who it was written for, how it was published, and so on.</q> I also think that's more fruitful than placing it within the history of the genre.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: OK, that sounds reasonable.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: Could I ask for some advice about writing the paper I'm working on about the Vikings? I have to do that this week, and I'm a bit stuck.

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: Of course. Have you decided yet what to write about?

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: No, I haven't. There's so much that seems interesting – Viking settlement in other countries, trade, mythology...

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: Well, <q id="26">what I suggest is that you read an assignment a student wrote last year,</q> which is kept in the library. It's short and well focused, and I'm sure you'll find it helpful. I'll give you the details in a moment. Textbooks usually cover so many topics, it can be very difficult to choose just one.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: OK. I've got a DVD of the film about the Vikings that came out earlier this year. Should I watch that again?

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: If it's the one I am thinking of, hmm, I'd ignore it – it's more fantasy than reality. But <q id="27">I've got a recording of a documentary that you should watch.</q> It makes some interesting and provocative points, which I think will help you to focus your topic.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: <q id="28">So then should I work out an outline?</q>

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: <q id="28">Yes. Just headings for different sections, at this stage.</q> And <q id="29">then you should start looking for suitable articles and books to draw on, and take notes</q> which you organise according to those headings.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: I see.

transcript.speaker: BETH
transcript.text: <q id="30">Then put short phrases and sentences as bullet points under each heading.</q> Make sure that this skeleton makes sense and flows properly, before writing up the paper in full.

transcript.speaker: JAMES
transcript.text: OK. Thanks, that's very helpful.

Over the years, attitudes towards workers have changed considerably. After all, there was a time when workers had no rights at all, and laboured in appalling conditions. Conditions have improved a lot, but conflict in the workplace is still common. And human resources managers nowadays need to be able to deal with it when necessary.

<q id="31">What is conflict in the workplace? Definitions vary, but I'm taking it to refer to a whole range of behaviours that the victim finds unacceptable, from minor, harmless arguments to – at the opposite extreme – physical violence. Much of this is covered by the term bullying,</q> by which I mean one or more people behaving abusively or aggressively against another who is in a weaker position. Although all behaviour like this is a form of conflict, not all conflict can be described in these terms.

As with all human behaviour, there are numerous reasons for it. But <q id="32">often it's caused by someone who feels the need to show their superiority over someone else,</q> in order to feel that they aren't at the lowest level in a hierarchy or a group of people.

<q id="33">In some cases one person simply dislikes the other, on the basis that the personality of one is in some way incompatible with that of the other person.</q> A general habit of optimism in one person could make them intolerant of a colleague who's constantly pessimistic – not that that justifies treating them badly, of course.

<q id="34">Some conflicts arise when people are more interested in promoting themselves and their team than in the company as a whole. These conflicts are called 'structural',</q> and could come about, for example, when a sales team believe they are the only people in the business who do any useful work, and look down on behind-the-scenes administrators.

<q id="35">Conflict obviously affects the individuals concerned – the situation is likely to be very stressful for victims, resulting in their absence from work, possibly for months.</q> For the company, if no effort is made to deal with conflict, it can spiral out of control, and even lead to the breakdown of the business.

Some interesting work with chief executives – CEOs – has uncovered some of the reasons why they may treat colleagues badly. <q id="36">Many CEOs combine two opposing characteristics: confidence – that is, the belief that they're capable of great achievements – with a high level of anxiety,</q> a fear of missing targets, whether set by themselves or by the directors of the company. This combination can make them respond badly to anyone who questions their decisions.

In a high pressure work environment, such characteristics become problematic. And <q id="37">it's particularly difficult to tackle the situation where colleagues, managers and board members are all trying to achieve their own visions. When they can't agree on strategic issues and on where they see the business going,</q> there are real problems.

For managers at lower levels within the organisation, it might seem that an autocratic form of management – where the chief executive gives orders and everyone else has to obey – would see more conflict than others. Interestingly, though, <q id="38">a company with a more democratic business model, can suffer more, when uncertainty about who to report to leads to conflicting demands.</q>

Now I'll say a little about dealing with the type of conflict that has harmful effects. Of course the ideal is to prevent it arising in the first place. <q id="39">A good manager, at any level, will make efforts to earn the respect of the people they work with,</q> particularly those who report to them. That will involve politeness in all communications, and treating them as equals who happen to have a different role within the organisation.

Sometimes, of course, conflict does occur, and can get out of hand. In such cases the human resources department often gets involved. However, <q id="40">if one of the parties in a conflict sees human resources as simply a mouthpiece for the chief executive, then an external mediator might be able to help.</q> By talking to both sides, and trying to find the truth of what's been happening, they can build a clear picture of the situation, and give feedback that both sides will accept, precisely because they're independent.
